## Chapter 6: Quality

### Critical to Quality Characteristics

Critical to quality characteristics, or CTQs, are the factors or parameters that are the main drivers of quality within an organization or process. Generally, CTQs are key characteristics that can be measured; where the performance of that metric provides information about whether the customer will be satisfied or not.

CTQs are closely related to CTCs, or critical to customer characteristics, but they aren't the same thing. Something can be critical to quality — even critical to how the customer ultimately feels about a service or product — without being directly critical to the customer. CTQs are internal concerns, but they drive CTCs.

⁷ https://www.iso.org/obp/ui/#iso:std:iso:9000:ed-3:v1:en:term:3.9.11

Let's look at a few CTQ and CTC examples to understand the difference and relationship between these two factors.

**A Pair of Pants**

When a customer buys a pair of pants, they're generally concerned with fit and appearance. Are they comfortable, is the size correct, and does the garment match the customer's personal style?

It's hard to create a measurement for whether pants are comfortable, but a manufacturer can collect customer feedback on various types of pants and find that a particular fabric with a particular cut is the most comfortable for the target audience. The manufacturer can also determine the appropriate measurements for each size. During the manufacturing process, these critical to quality factors are applied: only fabric that meets the identified specifications is used. The fabric is then cut to specific measurements and sewn in a specific way — the measurements and sewing methods are critical to quality.

The average customer, though, doesn't want to hear about the exact measurements of every piece of fabric or how the seams were sewn. They want to put on a pair of pants and feel a comfortable fit.

**Chocolate Bars**

A chocolate company runs a survey to find out why sales of its newest product didn't perform as expected. The feedback suggests the chocolate is too sweet — the chocolate's flavor and sweetness are a critical to customer characteristic.

The company can adjust its formula, cutting the amount of sugar that goes into the chocolate. The recipe — and the amount of sugar — is a critical to quality factor in this case. But what if customer feedback indicated health-conscious consumers simply didn't want to buy a chocolate bar with that much sugar? Then the amount of sugar in the recipe becomes both a CTQ and a CTC. It's critical to the bar's flavor quality, but customers might also look at the nutrition information on the packaging and make purchasing decisions based on how much sugar is in the chocolate.

**Mobile App Development**

If a company wants to launch a mobile app for its customers, then an obvious customer-centered need is that the app work on the customer's phone. The customer doesn't care about the process the company has to go through to release the app on the platform in question, but the company needs to meet the criteria set by Apple, Android, Windows, or other mobile operating systems. These requirements become some of the CTQs for mobile app development, even though certain platform requirements might not seem at all related to customer statements about wants or needs.

#### Why Identify CTQs?

In a process improvement setting, CTQs are fundamental to narrowing the scope of the work and understanding how to drive change. Consider the 80/20 rule discussed in Chapter 8. Often, CTQs are the factors, characteristics, or outputs that drive 80% of customer satisfaction. By improving these few critical factors, teams can substantially impact customer satisfaction and overall process performance. Identifying CTQs lets teams create the largest possible improvement with the available time, money, and people resources.

Outside a project setting, understanding CTQs lets organizations keep quality on track. By managing a few critical metrics, teams can ensure excellent outcomes on an ongoing basis and identify potential improvement areas before they become customer-visible problems.

#### Using a CTQ Tree to Convert Customer Needs into Quality Metrics

In Chapter 8, we introduced the concept of Voice of the Customer, or VoC. Six Sigma teams generally start with some kind of VoC data when defining a problem and working on goals for a project. Either the team runs surveys to hear from a statistically relevant group of customers during a project's early phases, or the team gets feedback from internal customers about a process. Sometimes the VoC information a team starts with is something as simple as a sponsor or executive-level individual making a statement about expectations for an internal process or project. When VoC data is limited this way, teams may have to work harder to validate assumptions with data before moving on to CTQ analysis.

To get a better understanding of how to measure a process's quality, teams need to convert VoC statements into CTQs. One of the best ways to do this is through a diagramming process known as a CTQ tree.

A CTQ tree starts with specific, critical customer needs, breaks that need down into drivers, and uses the drivers to build requirements. Specific requirements are easier to convert into measurable quality components. Although every CTQ tree is unique, they all start with a common shape. The common structure of a CTQ tree is shown below.

When building a CTQ tree, you don't need to follow an equal pattern for drivers and requirements. Some customer needs will have more drivers than others; some drivers will have more requirements. You might also have several CTQ trees — you'll want to build one for each need identified as critical to a customer.

**Identify Critical Customer Needs**

Start the CTQ tree process by building a list of critical customer needs. A bank working on processes related to online checking account access might identify accessibility, user-friendly interfaces, and information security as the main critical customer needs, for example. Define the needs in broad terms to help capture every driver and requirement further along in the diagramming process.

The best way to define needs is to ask customers directly for feedback, but time and resources don't always allow for surveys. Six Sigma teams can draw on data collected through recent surveys or feedback forms, which is the second-best option. In the absence of customer feedback, brainstorm critical needs with a group of employees who have knowledge and experience with the customer. Subject-matter experts from sales, customer service, and complaint departments can often provide actionable information when the customer is the end user. You can also start a CTQ tree with the outputs from your SIPOC diagram; depending on how you structured the outputs on a SIPOC, you might need to define critical quality factors for the output as a starting point for your CTQ tree diagram.

**Identify Quality Drivers**

Once you have a list of critical needs, work through one need at a time to build a tree similar to the diagram above. Identify the quality drivers that need to be present or met for the customer need to be satisfied. For example, an HVAC service company's customers might require excellent service. The drivers for that need might include friendly service technicians, helpful and knowledgeable staff, and a fast response to service calls.

Drivers are the transition point between customer needs and requirements; you don't necessarily need to be able to measure the drivers, but you want them to be somewhat more detailed than the broad customer needs already identified, and you want them to flow toward measurable factors whenever possible.

**List Requirements for Each Driver**

Requirements are the most detailed breakdown with respect to critical to quality characteristics. They're the things you can measure, that let you understand whether the drivers are performing adequately, so that customer needs are met.

For example, let's look at our HVAC example in CTQ tree format.

You can see in the CTQ tree above that the drivers were converted into requirements — and each of these requirements can be measured with numbers. In some cases, driver-to-requirement conversions come down to a fixed number. The chocolate bar example at the start of this chapter presents a scenario like that: if the company determines that the recipe with a quarter cup of sugar is the correct recipe, then the process metric for quality is exactly a quarter cup of sugar.

In other examples, companies might allow room for exceptions or the understanding that a process won't hit an exact number every time. For example, an HVAC team can't possibly arrive at a customer's home exactly 24 hours after a call is placed — and if service technicians can arrive before 24 hours, most people would be happy about that. That means the company needs to build a definition for the requirement: how many hours before a customer considers a technician late? For our example company, it's 48 hours. The requirement in another situation might be 24 hours.

Since teams will use the requirements from CTQ trees to develop process success measurements and metrics, it's extremely important that every requirement be verified before teams build it into the project or process. Requirements should be checked against VoC data, existing measurements, and the experience and knowledge of subject-matter experts and leaders. The team should ask itself, and ask others: "If these requirements are met, will the customer be satisfied?" If the answer is no at any point, then the requirements need adjusting. The team might also consider asking: "Are these requirements possible in the real world?" If the answer is no, then the process or the requirements need work.

### CoQ and CoPQ

Six Sigma teams should always be aware that quality has a cost. When talking about quality costs, many organizations consider what's known as the cost of poor quality, or CoPQ. The cost of poor quality is defined as the costs or expenses associated with the defects a process creates. Quality actually has a broader cost — avoiding poor quality also has a cost. The cost of quality, or CoQ, covers the expenses associated with maintaining good quality across an entire organization or process. This is sometimes called the cost of good quality. In this section, we'll talk about both types of cost measurement, how they relate to Six Sigma in general, and how they relate to Six Sigma teams and projects.

#### The Cost of Poor Quality

In a way, the cost of poor quality is easier to measure than the cost associated with overall quality. CoPQ is generally split into two main categories: costs associated with external failures and costs associated with internal failures. External and internal failures are often called nonconformance costs — they're the expenses that occur when outputs don't meet critical to quality requirements.

**External Failures**

External failures generally happen after products or services have been delivered, which means they're directly tied to customer dissatisfaction. External failures can include revenue losses tied to a drop in sales because of product, service, system, or information quality. Other types of external losses include expenses tied to repairs, returns, or rework associated with a customer complaint; expenses tied to warranties; or lost revenue or sales because of customer ill will or negative word of mouth.

**Internal Failures**

Internal failures happen when products, services, or processes don't meet the requirements the company has set, and the product or service is delivered to the customer in an unsatisfactory state. Internal failures are generally handled by scrapping the work, redoing the work, or repairing the work. Obviously, this rework results in extra material and labor costs, but it also results in losses tied to delays, part or stock shortages, and a lack of flexibility or adaptability. For example, if a process has such poor quality that 50% of the items it produces need rework, then the process might be producing 40% less daily than it could. That means the process can serve fewer customers, generate less output, and contribute less to the company's overall profit.

**Calculating the Cost of Poor Quality**

Understanding the cost of poor quality is fundamental for Six Sigma organizations, because it lets leaders understand how financial needs relate to the need for quality improvements. The higher the cost of poor quality, the more likely an organization is to work toward improvement.

At the project or process level, the cost of poor quality can help determine improvement budgets. If poor quality within the process is costing an organization $5,000 a month, a project that costs $20,000 but saves $3,000 a month in quality would pay for itself in just seven months. On the other hand, a project that costs $100,000 when the costs of poor quality are only $1,000 a month is less likely to make sense.

The equation for CoPQ is:

**CoPQ = External Failure Costs + Internal Failure Costs**

Although the equation looks simple, identifying every cost associated with poor quality can be hard. Most specialists use the iceberg metaphor to explain the hidden costs of poor quality. On the surface, you see the small tip of the iceberg — the obvious costs of poor quality. These might be things like scrap, reprocessing, warranty claims, customer returns, and extra shipping.

Below the surface, though, an iceberg is always much bigger. The same is generally true for the cost of poor quality, and the hidden costs can include:

- Loss of customer loyalty
- Loss of morale
- Loss of employees if morale stays low for extended periods
- Conflicts tied to scheduling or rescheduling
- Higher risks of compliance problems, including fines
- Higher administrative costs
- Unpredictable revenue, sales, or production

Calculating the cost of poor quality is extremely hard at the company level and still moderately hard at the process level. There's no method for listing every possible cost and formalizing it into dollar values. It's a good idea for organizations to develop a simplified method used company-wide when calculating CoPQ. At minimum, the Six Sigma specialists in the organization might consider defining a specific way to list poor-quality costs company-wide, so that various process teams use similar measures when reporting to leadership.

#### The Cost of Quality

The cost of quality, or CoQ, includes the cost of poor quality and the cost of good quality. Beyond internal and external failure costs, CoQ includes prevention and appraisal costs. Prevention and appraisal costs are often called conformance costs — they're the expenses tied to making sure outputs meet critical to quality requirements.

**Prevention Costs**

Prevention costs are the expenses tied to any activity aimed at keeping an error or defect from occurring. Error-proofing, covered in detail in later chapters on process control, results in prevention costs. For example, if a company makes baked goods, at some point in the process people or machines need to measure the ingredients to be added to dough batches. One way to error-proof such a process is to provide specialized machinery that only allows a specific amount of each ingredient to be introduced into a batch. Such a machine would likely be fairly expensive; it would also have to be operated by a trained operator and maintained by proper repair and cleaning staff. All that activity would generate costs that could be considered preventive in nature.

Other types of prevention costs include expenses tied to quality planning, reviews, or quality-focused education and training. Quality review and evaluation processes also create prevention costs, whether those reviews relate to suppliers, products, processes, or people. Customer surveys, creating technical manuals, the work of building and managing requirements and specifications, and managing job descriptions can all lead to prevention costs. Even cleaning costs can be considered prevention costs, especially if a clean work environment is needed to reduce failures or errors in manufacturing products.

**Appraisal Costs**

Appraisal costs are those tied to any activity aimed at ensuring high quality levels within a process or organization. If a manufacturing plant hires a quality control specialist, and that person's job is to review parts coming down the manufacturing line and send work back for correction or report the quality level as a metric, then that person's salary and any expenses tied to their employment are appraisal costs. In some cases, these expenses could also be considered prevention costs, but they wouldn't be counted twice when calculating CoQ.

Other types of appraisal costs can include expenses tied to quality audits of products, services, or processes, the cost of calibration and measurement equipment or software, and the costs of field testing. Prototype inspections, consulting expenses, financial reporting and auditing, safety checks, job-safety checks, supplier certifications, employee surveys, and customer feedback are all additional examples of areas where appraisal costs might exist.

**Calculating the Cost of Quality**

The equation for CoQ is:

**CoQ = CoPQ + Prevention Costs + Appraisal Costs**

The same challenges inherent in calculating CoPQ also exist when calculating CoQ. The same iceberg analogy applies, and prevention and appraisal activities often carry hidden costs, like unnecessary overtime, paperwork, or system expenses.

#### The Cost of Quality and Six Sigma

Conventional wisdom might say that, if the cost of poor quality drops, the cost of good quality is likely to rise. You have to spend money on quality to have good quality, in other words. Although this may historically be true for many organizations, it isn't the case at a Six Sigma company. Since Six Sigma works to build quality into the process itself — meaning things are done right the first time and defects are reduced — quality costs often drop while quality itself rises.

In Chapter 2, we showed that a process with a higher sigma level (and therefore higher quality) has fewer defects. Defects drop exponentially as the sigma level rises. Since there are fewer defects, the costs of poor quality are also exponentially reduced. But time and again, Six Sigma has also reduced the cost of overall quality. As the sigma level of processes rises through the application of Six Sigma tools and methodology, the cost of both prevention and appraisal also drops.

One way to relate the cost of quality — and perhaps the most common way to do so among corporations — is as a percentage of sales. The cost of quality as a percentage of sales typically aligns so closely with sigma values that you can predict the cost of quality based on a company's or process's sigma value. The average CoQ ranges relative to sigma values are shown in the table below. As you can see, as companies improve their sigma levels, they experience substantial savings in the cost of quality.

#### Managing the Cost of Quality

Six Sigma is one of the best methodologies for managing the cost of quality because it works to build quality into every process. When addressing an organization or process with a high cost of quality, teams and leadership can apply a triage-based method to reduce those costs. Although no organization can eliminate quality costs 100%, the goal should be zero failure costs, whether internal or external, and minimal prevention and appraisal costs.

First, teams should focus on costs associated with failures. It's often easier and less expensive to spot costs tied to nonconformance, and improvements aimed at fixing the causes of a few critical failures can have a big impact on overall quality and total cost. Instead of layering quality programs on top of processes to ensure quality — which just adds prevention or appraisal activities and raises the cost of quality — Six Sigma improvement projects build preventive measures into the processes themselves. In other words, efficient Six Sigma processes are self-regulating. They have built-in checks and balances that work to constantly reduce defects and rework.

The benefits of building failure stop-points into a process include:

- Earlier detection when errors occur, which keeps hidden costs low. When the error can't reach the next process or the customer, you avoid a lot of problems and costs tied to low morale, reduced customer loyalty, or product returns.
- Employees can better support and manage higher quality. When quality is something employees take ownership of, they're more likely to work hard to create the best possible outcome. In contrast, appraisal-style quality programs can trigger feelings of paranoia from being closely watched, or create a link in employees' minds between the idea of quality and the idea of retaliation or correction. Ongoing poor performance genuinely needs to be addressed, but employees shouldn't adopt a negative mindset when hearing the word quality.
- Quality assurance built into the process is actually more effective than post-process or over-process prevention and appraisal methods. Statistical process control and Six Sigma improvements can bring a process to the six sigma level. To ensure the same level of performance — 3.4 defects per million opportunities — quality assurance staff would need to review millions of parts and make sure only a tiny fraction had defects. It simply isn't an economical option for most, if not all, organizations.

After teams use the Six Sigma and Lean management methods discussed throughout this book to reduce failure costs, teams can turn their attention to prevention and appraisal costs. Often, in a process running at a high sigma level, prevention and appraisal activities are a form of muda. They can be eliminated from the process without impacting the end product, quality, customer satisfaction, or employee morale. In some cases, removing prevention or appraisal from processes actually creates a positive impact on quality, output, and customer and employee satisfaction.

**Identifying Prevention and Appraisal Activities**

The first step in removing quality-related muda is identifying it. Process maps, spaghetti diagrams, and value stream maps are valuable tools for uncovering activities that don't need to be included in a process. All these tools are covered in depth in PART XIV.

Whether mapping a process or simply discussing various components with process owners or a Six Sigma team, asking questions about value and necessity can also help identify prevention and appraisal muda. If you think an activity related to a process might be an unnecessary form of prevention or appraisal, ask:

- Does the activity itself add any value to the output?
- Does the activity substantially reduce the time needed for the process to produce an output?
- Does the activity substantially raise the process's cost?
- If the activity is designed to prevent defects within the process, can it be made more efficient?
- If the activity is designed to prevent defects, can it be made less expensive?
- If an activity is designed to capture quality data about the process for reporting purposes, are those reports needed?
- If quality reports are needed — whether because of mandatory requirements, like compliance, or because the reports provide value in another process — can the reports be automated to reduce the associated expenses?

The answers to these questions help teams identify areas where muda can be removed or where quality-related processes can be improved.

### Quality Is Fundamental to Success

When Six Sigma teams are eliminating quality-related costs and unnecessary activities from processes, it's critical that they don't remove quality itself. Although it's true that traditional quality programs and costs don't need to be present to ensure a reduction in defects and an improvement in customer satisfaction, it's equally true that you need to replace those programs with some other form of control. By the end of this book, you'll have learned about a range of tools, from statistical process control to poka yokes, that you can use to build quality into a process.

It's also worth noting that a single Six Sigma team — or even an entire department dedicated to Six Sigma — can't reduce quality costs at an organization on its own. Corporate leadership needs to buy into the belief that quality is better when controls are built into the process, and needs to be willing to communicate that fact through training and example. Some companies instead choose to use Six Sigma to improve processes while still maintaining the expense of traditional quality, compliance, and audit departments. For some sectors, like healthcare or finance, audits and other appraisal and prevention costs may be required by laws and regulations. Outside that mandate, it's almost always better to remove any quality activity that doesn't provide added value.
